QF.id: AIFM CIII Fee Structure and Fund Performance_41

question.text: For a well-diversified Cat III equity long-only sub-strategy, the Sharpe Ratio and Treynor Ratio will typically give:

answer.text: Identical numbers because they use the same formula
Similar rankings because, in a well-diversified portfolio, unsystematic risk is small and β ≈ σ/σ_market
Treynor will always be higher than Sharpe

explanation.text: **The Logic:** When a portfolio is well-diversified, unsystematic risk is close to zero, so total σ is dominated by the systematic component. Sharpe (uses σ) and Treynor (uses β) will give SIMILAR rankings. For undiversified/concentrated portfolios they diverge. **The Trap:** A overstates divergence. B confuses formulas. D is arbitrary. **Cross-Exam Context:** This distinction is a favourite XV Research Analyst question. XIX-E tests Cat III context — concentrated long-short funds often show Sharpe/Treynor divergence. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** If your long-short book shows big Sharpe-vs-Treynor divergence, investigate whether you're running too-concentrated factor exposures (e.g., unintended big beta to small-cap). LPs dislike hidden factor bets.
